    1: \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
    2: 
    3: Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
    4: 
    5: Our starting point is the extension chain
    6: \[
    7: \mathbb{L}_0 \xhookrightarrow{\iota} \mathbb{L}_1 \preceq \mathbb{L}_2 \preceq \mathbb{L}_3 \preceq \mathbb{L}_4,
    8: \]
    9: where $\mathbb{L}_0$ is the pointwise layer, $\mathbb{L}_1$ is the information-state forcing layer, $\mathbb{L}_2$ adds local objects and site structure, $\mathbb{L}_3$ adds branchwise obstruction data, and $\mathbb{L}_4$ adds refinement dynamics. The map $\mathbb{L}_0\hookrightarrow\mathbb{L}_1$ is a singleton semantic embedding, whereas the later steps are conservative extensions in the sense of \Cref{def:conservative-extension}. Thus the geometric and homological material introduced later does not alter the forcing behaviour of formulas already present in the lower layers.
   10: The semantics is thus related both to team and imperfect-information semantics \cite{Hodges1997,Vaananen2007,AbramskyPuljujarviVaananen2025} and to the forcing and sheaf-theoretic tradition stemming from Beth, Kripke, Fitting, and Tierney and later developed in topos-theoretic form \cite{Beth1956,Kripke1965,Fitting1969,Tierney1972,Goldblatt2006,Johnstone2002}.
   11: 
   12: The first part of the paper concerns the passage from information states to local objects. \Cref{prop:compsec-to-sheafification} shows that compatible local sectionability gives nonemptiness of the associated sheafification, and \Cref{thm:sheafification-characterization} proves the converse on slice-separated reference slices. We then prove in \Cref{thm:pointwise-irreducibility} that the predicates $\CompSec_s$, $\Sec_s$, and $\Null^{\mathrm{glue}}_s$ are not definable by automorphism-invariant, constant-free formulas of the $\mathbb{L}_1$-reduct with one free reference variable. This is only a lower-bound statement for the comparison fragment under consideration, but it isolates a genuine change of behaviour between $\mathbb L_1$ and $\mathbb L_2$.
   13: 
   14: The second part begins once the set-valued local-object functor is enriched by groupoid-valued data. \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} gives a rigidity statement for representative-rigid lifts: if the local-object presheaf is slice-separated and a realization prestack admits a strict functorial choice of representatives and is globally conservative at the terminal fibre, then the sheafification unit is surjective there; under $H^1$-vanishing and the same slice-separatedness, this is equivalent to the local object functor already being a sheaf at the terminal fibre. Thus gluing-level nullity is necessarily tied to genuinely gluing-sensitive lift data. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} identifies the canonicity that survives at this level: once the sheafified local object functor has been lifted to a banded realization stack, the branch obstruction map to derived $H^2$ is intrinsic up to equivalence of banded extensions. For such an extension, visible value classes are the global sections of the sheaf of connected components (\Cref{thm:visible-value-components}), each visible branch determines a banded component gerbe (\Cref{thm:component-gerbe-decomposition}), and, on slice-separated reference slices, \Cref{thm:gerbe-null-semantics} identifies gluing-level absence with the existence of visible branches together with non-neutrality of the corresponding component gerbes.
   15: 
   16: The empirical-model interface gives a sharp limit to this canonicity.  \Cref{thm:empirical-model-stack-interface} proves that every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical split realization-stack extension, pseudonatural under ordinary refinements of measurement contexts, but every component gerbe in that extension is neutral.  The Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa class is a relative \v{C}ech $H^1$ class of a presheaf, equivalently a torsor class \cite{AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,Caru2017}; it is indexed by a chosen local section.  By contrast, the Giraud map here is a derived $H^2$ class for a sheaf band, indexed by a global component, and for a strongly contextual model that indexing set is empty.  Thus the canonical split construction supplies no non-split banded data, and no branch map of the present kind can recover the AMB classes on all finite empirical models without an additional degree-shifting construction. Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ghz} exhibits only a chosen split GHZ/Mermin lift.
   17: 
   18: The homological part of the paper starts only after one visible branch, one finite nerve presentation, and one constant finite abelian band have been fixed. From that point the tools are classical: the universal coefficient sequence, finite-abelian duality, and standard quotient arguments. What matters for the semantics, at a fixed presentation, is the presentation-object image
   19: \[
   20: K_\omega:=\operatorname{Im}(\mathrm{ev}_\omega)
   21: \]
   22: and quotient $A_{\mathrm{vis}}^\omega=A/K_\omega$ attached to the branch obstruction class. \Cref{prop:invariance-visible-quotients} establishes invariance under elementary homology-equivalent refinements, cocycle replacement, and re-trivialization of the band, and gives functorial transport along chosen finite comparison zigzags; it does not assert path independence between distinct zigzags. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-visible-quotient} gives the corresponding character-theoretic description, and \Cref{thm:character-blind-obstructions} identifies the character-blind case with the pure $\operatorname{Ext}$ contribution.
   23: 
   24: When several visible branches are present, one obtains branch-sensitive and branch-uniform quotients, related by the short exact sequence of \Cref{thm:branch-comparison-exact-sequence}. On a generated pullback subsite for a fixed finite nerve, with constant finite abelian band, the explicit finite-site Leray comparison of \Cref{lem:generated-subsite-model-interface}, and the additional assumption $H_1(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak=0$, we prove realization theorems for prescribed branchwise homomorphisms $H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak\to A$. These theorems are internal constructions under the generated admissible-expansion convention of \Cref{prop:admissible-layer-expansion-interface}: the algebraic data are built first, and the one-state $\mathbb L_2$- and $\mathbb L_3$-models are then obtained by admissible expansion. \Cref{thm:prescribed-branch-realization} treats non-neutral branches, while \Cref{thm:mixed-branch-realization} allows arbitrary finite families and identifies the neutral branches with the zero maps.
   25: 
   26: Under the same fixed finite-nerve, constant-band, $H_1=0$, and mixed-realization hypotheses, if $H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\cong \mathbb Z^\beta$, \Cref{cor:torsion-free-h2-classification} shows that the realizable hidden subgroups are exactly the subgroups of $A$ generated by at most $\beta$ elements. The bouquet theorem \Cref{thm:bouquet-two-branch-resolution} then supplies an explicit chosen family of examples, namely open-star good covers of a fixed finite model of $\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2$, for which the acyclic-cover hypothesis is automatic and the pure two-branch resolution kernels can be classified explicitly: a finite abelian group $G$ occurs precisely when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group. This is an existence and classification statement inside the chosen good-cover construction, not a uniqueness assertion for all presentations of the bouquet and, by \Cref{thm:unique-branch-contextuality-comparison}, not an invariant canonically attached to empirical models.
   27: 
   28: The sheaf-theoretic, gerbe-theoretic, and homological tools used here are classical, and several of the later comparison results are formal once the branchwise intrinsic data have been fixed. The contribution of the paper is accordingly structural: the extension chain separates the semantic layers, the empirical-model comparison proves exactly where an extra categorical degree enters, and the obstruction class gives rise to a groupoid-indexed invariant only after branchwise lift data and a finite nerve presentation have been fixed.
   29: 
   30: The paper is organized as follows. \Cref{sec:preliminaries} fixes the extension chain and the relevant notions of conservativity. \Cref{sec:information-states} recalls forcing over information states. \Cref{sec:null-decomposition} studies local objects, sheafification, and lower-fragment separation. \Cref{sec:gerbe-obstruction} introduces component gerbes and branch obstruction classes. \Cref{sec:homological-visibility} and \Cref{sec:branch-aggregation} contain the homological visibility theory together with the branchwise comparison and realization results. The appendix collects the supplementary material on refinement dynamics and the GHZ/Mermin example.

main.tex:70:We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a Giraud class in $H^2$. Every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical refinement-functorial split extension, but all its Giraud classes vanish; the Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction is instead a relative $H^1$ torsor class indexed by a local section. sec_conclusion.tex:5:At the passage from set-valued to groupoid-valued data, \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} shows that a slice-separated representative-rigid lift can be globally conservative only when the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre is surjective; under $H^1$-vanishing and slice-separatedness on the reference slice, this is equivalent to sheafiness of the local object functor at that fibre. Thus the gerbe-theoretic part of the theory is necessarily relative to additional lift data. \Cref{thm:empirical-model-stack-interface} makes this limitation exact for finite empirical models: their support presheaves have canonical refinement-functorial split realization stacks with neutral component gerbes. The AMB class is instead the degree-one class of a torsor indexed by a local section, and cannot be recovered for all finite models by the branchwise Giraud map, whose domain is empty for strongly contextual models. Once a non-split banded extension is separately supplied, \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} gives the maximal remaining canonicity: the branch obstruction class is intrinsic up to equivalence of such extensions.

sec_introduction.tex:3:Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
sec_introduction.tex:14:The second part begins once the set-valued local-object functor is enriched by groupoid-valued data. \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} gives a rigidity statement for representative-rigid lifts: if the local-object presheaf is slice-separated and a realization prestack admits a strict functorial choice of representatives and is globally conservative at the terminal fibre, then the sheafification unit is surjective there; under $H^1$-vanishing and the same slice-separatedness, this is equivalent to the local object functor already being a sheaf at the terminal fibre. Thus gluing-level nullity is necessarily tied to genuinely gluing-sensitive lift data. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} identifies the canonicity that survives at this level: once the sheafified local object functor has been lifted to a banded realization stack, the branch obstruction map to derived $H^2$ is intrinsic up to equivalence of banded extensions. For such an extension, visible value classes are the global sections of the sheaf of connected components (\Cref{thm:visible-value-components}), each visible branch determines a banded component gerbe (\Cref{thm:component-gerbe-decomposition}), and, on slice-separated reference slices, \Cref{thm:gerbe-null-semantics} identifies gluing-level absence with the existence of visible branches together with non-neutrality of the corresponding component gerbes.
sec_introduction.tex:16:The empirical-model interface gives a sharp limit to this canonicity.  \Cref{thm:empirical-model-stack-interface} proves that every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical split realization-stack extension, pseudonatural under ordinary refinements of measurement contexts, but every component gerbe in that extension is neutral.  The Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa class is a relative \v{C}ech $H^1$ class of a presheaf, equivalently a torsor class \cite{AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,Caru2017}; it is indexed by a chosen local section.  By contrast, the Giraud map here is a derived $H^2$ class for a sheaf band, indexed by a global component, and for a strongly contextual model that indexing set is empty.  Thus the canonical split construction supplies no non-split banded data, and no branch map of the present kind can recover the AMB classes on all finite empirical models without an additional degree-shifting construction. Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ghz} exhibits only a chosen split GHZ/Mermin lift.
sec_introduction.tex:24:When several visible branches are present, one obtains branch-sensitive and branch-uniform quotients, related by the short exact sequence of \Cref{thm:branch-comparison-exact-sequence}. On a generated pullback subsite for a fixed finite nerve, with constant finite abelian band, the explicit finite-site Leray comparison of \Cref{lem:generated-subsite-model-interface}, and the additional assumption $H_1(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak=0$, we prove realization theorems for prescribed branchwise homomorphisms $H_2(N(\mathcal U),\mathbb Z)\allowbreak\to A$. These theorems are internal constructions under the generated admissible-expansion convention of \Cref{prop:admissible-layer-expansion-interface}: the algebraic data are built first, and the one-state $\mathbb L_2$- and $\mathbb L_3$-models are then obtained by admissible expansion. \Cref{thm:prescribed-branch-realization} treats non-neutral branches, while \Cref{thm:mixed-branch-realization} allows arbitrary finite families and identifies the neutral branches with the zero maps.

sec_introduction.tex:3:Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
sec_introduction.tex:9:where $\mathbb{L}_0$ is the pointwise layer, $\mathbb{L}_1$ is the information-state forcing layer, $\mathbb{L}_2$ adds local objects and site structure, $\mathbb{L}_3$ adds branchwise obstruction data, and $\mathbb{L}_4$ adds refinement dynamics. The map $\mathbb{L}_0\hookrightarrow\mathbb{L}_1$ is a singleton semantic embedding, whereas the later steps are conservative extensions in the sense of \Cref{def:conservative-extension}. Thus the geometric and homological material introduced later does not alter the forcing behaviour of formulas already present in the lower layers.

main.tex:58:\title[Gluing Obstructions and Homological Visibility]{Gluing Obstructions and Homological Visibility in a State-Forcing Semantics}
main.tex:70:We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a Giraud class in $H^2$. Every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical refinement-functorial split extension, but all its Giraud classes vanish; the Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction is instead a relative $H^1$ torsor class indexed by a local section. Thus the banded theory requires extra lift data. For finite abelian bands its homological evaluation map controls a presentation-object visible quotient. On bouquet good covers, a nonzero finite abelian group occurs as a pure two-branch resolution kernel exactly when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group, but this classification does not canonically transfer to empirical models.

main.tex:70:We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a Giraud class in $H^2$. Every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical refinement-functorial split extension, but all its Giraud classes vanish; the Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction is instead a relative $H^1$ torsor class indexed by a local section. Thus the banded theory requires extra lift data. For finite abelian bands its homological evaluation map controls a presentation-object visible quotient. On bouquet good covers, a nonzero finite abelian group occurs as a pure two-branch resolution kernel exactly when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group, but this classification does not canonically transfer to empirical models.
sec_conclusion.tex:5:At the passage from set-valued to groupoid-valued data, \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} shows that a slice-separated representative-rigid lift can be globally conservative only when the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre is surjective; under $H^1$-vanishing and slice-separatedness on the reference slice, this is equivalent to sheafiness of the local object functor at that fibre. Thus the gerbe-theoretic part of the theory is necessarily relative to additional lift data. \Cref{thm:empirical-model-stack-interface} makes this limitation exact for finite empirical models: their support presheaves have canonical refinement-functorial split realization stacks with neutral component gerbes. The AMB class is instead the degree-one class of a torsor indexed by a local section, and cannot be recovered for all finite models by the branchwise Giraud map, whose domain is empty for strongly contextual models. Once a non-split banded extension is separately supplied, \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} gives the maximal remaining canonicity: the branch obstruction class is intrinsic up to equivalence of such extensions.

sec_introduction.tex:12:The first part of the paper concerns the passage from information states to local objects. \Cref{prop:compsec-to-sheafification} shows that compatible local sectionability gives nonemptiness of the associated sheafification, and \Cref{thm:sheafification-characterization} proves the converse on slice-separated reference slices. We then prove in \Cref{thm:pointwise-irreducibility} that the predicates $\CompSec_s$, $\Sec_s$, and $\Null^{\mathrm{glue}}_s$ are not definable by automorphism-invariant, constant-free formulas of the $\mathbb{L}_1$-reduct with one free reference variable. sec_introduction.tex:14:The second part begins once the set-valued local-object functor is enriched by groupoid-valued data. \Cref{thm:canonical-lift-rigidity} gives a rigidity statement for representative-rigid lifts: if the local-object presheaf is slice-separated and a realization prestack admits a strict functorial choice of representatives and is globally conservative at the terminal fibre, then the sheafification unit is surjective there; under $H^1$-vanishing and the same slice-separatedness, this is equivalent to the local object functor already being a sheaf at the terminal fibre. Thus gluing-level nullity is necessarily tied to genuinely gluing-sensitive lift data. \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} identifies the canonicity that survives at this level: once the sheafified local object functor has been lifted to a banded realization stack, the branch obstruction map to derived $H^2$ is intrinsic up to equivalence of banded extensions. For such an extension, visible value classes are the global sections of the sheaf of connected components (\Cref{thm:visible-value-components}), each visible branch determines a banded component gerbe (\Cref{thm:component-gerbe-decomposition}), and, on slice-separated reference slices, \Cref{thm:gerbe-null-semantics} identifies gluing-level absence with the existence of visible branches together with non-neutrality of the corresponding component gerbes.
sec_introduction.tex:30:The paper is organized as follows. \Cref{sec:preliminaries} fixes the extension chain and the relevant notions of conservativity. \Cref{sec:information-states} recalls forcing over information states. \Cref{sec:null-decomposition} studies local objects, sheafification, and lower-fragment separation. \Cref{sec:gerbe-obstruction} introduces component gerbes and branch obstruction classes. \Cref{sec:homological-visibility} and \Cref{sec:branch-aggregation} contain the homological visibility theory together with the branchwise comparison and realization results.  \begin{document}
 
 \begin{abstract}
-We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a Giraud class in $H^2$. Every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical refinement-functorial split extension, but all its Giraud classes vanish; the Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction is instead a relative $H^1$ torsor class indexed by a local section. Thus the banded theory requires extra lift data. For finite abelian bands its homological evaluation map controls a presentation-object visible quotient. On bouquet good covers, a nonzero finite abelian group occurs as a pure two-branch resolution kernel exactly when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group, but this classification does not canonically transfer to empirical models.
+A nonzero finite abelian group $G$ occurs as a two-component label-loss kernel with complementary nonzero image subgroups on the chosen good-cover site of a wedge of $\beta$ copies of $S^2$ if and only if $d(G)\leq 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group.  This follows from the universal coefficient theorem after fixing a finite nerve, a constant finite abelian band, and a banded groupoid lift of a presheaf.  For a component-gerbe class $\omega$, evaluation on $H_2$ gives $\operatorname{ev}_\omega:H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A$; its image and cokernel determine the componentwise and aggregate quotients.  When $H_1(N,\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^\beta$, the possible image subgroups are exactly those generated by at most $\beta$ elements.  Under explicit separatedness, representability, and \v{C}ech-to-derived comparison hypotheses, matching families without global amalgamations correspond to non-neutral component gerbes.  This derived $H^2$ invariant is not the relative \v{C}ech $H^1$ obstruction of Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa; only the underlying support-presheaf comparison is functorial.
 \end{abstract}

    3: We fix the semantic framework used throughout. In particular, we distinguish conservative extension from the weaker singleton embedding that links the pointwise layer to information-state forcing.
    4: 
    5: \subsection*{Standing notation}
    6: States are denoted by $p,q,u$, and admitted references by $r:\mathsf{Ref}_s$ with associated class $a=[r]_p$. The local reference site at a state and sort is $\mathcal C_{p,s}$, the local object functor is $F_{p,s}$, the visible value classes of a reference are $\Vis_{p,s}(r)$, and branch obstruction classes are denoted by $\omega$ or $\omega_v$. Subscripts such as $\mathrm{vis}$, $\mathrm{br}$, and $\mathrm{unif}$ consistently indicate visible, branch-sensitive, and branch-uniform quotients.
    7: 
    8: \begin{definition}[Logic layer]\label{def:logic-layer}
    9: A \emph{logic layer} is a tuple
   10: \[
   11: \mathbb{L}=(\Sigma,\mathrm{Form},\Mod,\St,\Vdash,\models),
   12: \]
   13: where $\Sigma$ is a signature, $\mathrm{Form}$ is the class of well-formed $\Sigma$-formulas, $\Mod$ is a class of admissible models, $\St$ assigns to every $M\in\Mod$ a nonempty set $\St(M)$ of states, $\Vdash$ is a forcing relation on model-state pairs, and $\models$ is the induced consequence relation defined by
   14: \[
   15: \Gamma\models\varphi
   16: \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   17: \forall M\in\Mod\;\forall p\in\St(M)\,
   18: \bigl(M,p\Vdash\Gamma \Rightarrow M,p\Vdash\varphi\bigr).
   19: \]
   20: \end{definition}
   21: 
   22: Forcing is the primitive notion; consequence is derived from it.
   23: 
   24: \begin{definition}[Conservative extension]\label{def:conservative-extension}
   25: Let
   26: \[
   27: \mathbb{L}_m=(\Sigma_m,\mathrm{Form}_m,\Mod_m,\St_m,\Vdash_m,\models_m)
   28: \quad\text{and}\quad
   29: \mathbb{L}_n=(\Sigma_n,\mathrm{Form}_n,\Mod_n,\St_n,\Vdash_n,\models_n)
   30: \]
   31: with $m<n$. We say that $\mathbb{L}_n$ is a \emph{conservative extension} of $\mathbb{L}_m$, written $\mathbb{L}_m\preceq\mathbb{L}_n$, if there exist
   32: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
   33: \item a language embedding $e_{m,n}:\Sigma_m\hookrightarrow\Sigma_n$,
   34: \item a forgetful functor $U_{n,m}:\Mod_n\to\Mod_m$,
   35: \item for every $M\in\Mod_n$, a state projection
   36: \[
   37: \pi^M_{n,m}:\St_n(M)\to \St_m\bigl(U_{n,m}(M)\bigr),
   38: \]
   39: \end{enumerate}
   40: such that for every $\varphi\in \mathrm{Form}_m$, every $M\in\Mod_n$, and every $p\in\St_n(M)$,
   41: \begin{equation}\label{eq:conservative-extension}
   42: M,p\Vdash_n \varphi
   43: \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   44: U_{n,m}(M),\pi^M_{n,m}(p)\Vdash_m \varphi.
   45: \end{equation}
   46: \end{definition}
   47: 
   48: Thus a higher layer may add coordinates or geometric data, but lower-layer formulas are interpreted unchanged after projection.
   49: 
   50: \begin{definition}[Singleton semantic embedding]\label{def:singleton-semantic-embedding}
   51: Let $\mathbb{L}_0=(\Sigma_0,\mathrm{Form}_0,\Mod_0,\St_0,\Vdash_0,\models_0)$ and $\mathbb{L}_1=(\Sigma_1,\mathrm{Form}_1,\Mod_1,\St_1,\Vdash_1,\models_1)$. We say that $\mathbb{L}_0$ \emph{embeds into $\mathbb{L}_1$ by a singleton semantic embedding}, written $\mathbb{L}_0\hookrightarrow\mathbb{L}_1$, if there exist
   52: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]

   54: \item a forgetful functor $U_{1,0}:\Mod_1\to\Mod_0$,

   56: \[
   57: \iota_{0,1}^M(\rho)\in\St_1(M)
   58: \]
   59: \end{enumerate}
   60: such that for every $\varphi\in\mathrm{Form}_0$,
   61: \begin{equation}\label{eq:singleton-semantic-embedding}
   62: M,\iota_{0,1}^M(\rho)\Vdash_1\varphi
   63: \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   64: U_{1,0}(M),\rho\Vdash_0\varphi.
   65: \end{equation}
   66: \end{definition}
   67: 
   68: A singleton semantic embedding is weaker than a conservative extension: it compares only singleton states, and no projection from arbitrary information states to pointwise states is required.
   69: 
   70: \begin{proposition}[Composition of conservative extensions]\label{prop:conservative-composition}
   71: If $\mathbb{L}_\ell\preceq\mathbb{L}_m$ and $\mathbb{L}_m\preceq\mathbb{L}_n$, then $\mathbb{L}_\ell\preceq\mathbb{L}_n$.
   72: \end{proposition}
   73: 
   74: \begin{proof}
   75: Compose the language embeddings and forgetful functors:
   76: \[
   77: e_{\ell,n}:=e_{m,n}\circ e_{\ell,m},
   78: \qquad
   79: U_{n,\ell}:=U_{m,\ell}\circ U_{n,m}.
   80: \]
   81: For every $M\in\Mod_n$, define
   82: \[
   83: \pi^M_{n,\ell}:=

   85: \]

   87: \[

   93: \]
   94: by two applications of \Cref{def:conservative-extension}. This is exactly the required conservativity condition.
   95: \end{proof}

    3: Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical models already have two categorical
    4: reformulations close to the question considered here. Car\`u identifies the
    5: degree-one cohomology used by Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa with torsors
    6: trivialized by the measurement cover \cite[Prop.~6.3]{Caru2017}. More recently,
    7: Barbosa, Kharoof, and Okay construct fully faithful functors from measurement
    8: scenarios to bundle and simplicial-bundle scenarios, together with natural
    9: isomorphisms on their empirical-model functors
   10: \cite{BarbosaKharoofOkay2024}. Neither construction produces a banded gerbe
   11: or a realization-stack extension in the sense of
   12: \Cref{def:realization-stack-extension}. The following comparison locates the
   13: gap precisely.
   14: 
   15: Let a \emph{finite measurement scenario} be a finite set \(X\), finite
   16: nonempty outcome sets \(O_x\) for \(x\in X\), and a finite antichain
   17: \(\mathcal M\) of subsets of \(X\) whose union is \(X\). Write
   18: \(\mathcal D_{\mathcal M}\) for the finite context category consisting of
   19: the subcontexts of members of \(\mathcal M\), with inclusions as arrows, and
   20: equip it with the coverage induced by the maximal contexts. We also use its
   21: terminal augmentation, obtained by adjoining \(X\) and declaring
   22: \(\mathcal M\) to cover \(X\). A finite empirical model
   23: \[
   24: e=(e_C)_{C\in\mathcal M}
   25: \]
   26: is a compatible family of probability distributions on
   27: \(\prod_{x\in C}O_x\). Its support presheaf is
   28: \[
   29: S_e(U)=\operatorname{supp}(e_U)
   30: \qquad(U\in\mathcal D_{\mathcal M}),
   31: \]
   32: where compatibility makes the marginal \(e_U\) independent of the maximal
   33: context containing \(U\) \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011}. At the adjoined
   34: terminal object we take the right Kan extension
   35: \[
   36: \widehat S_e(X):=
   37: \varprojlim_{U\in\mathcal D_{\mathcal M}}S_e(U).
   38: \]
   39: Thus an element of \(\widehat S_e(X)\) is, by definition, a compatible family
   40: of supported local assignments. Below \(aS_e\) denotes the sheafification of
   41: this terminally augmented presheaf.
   42: 
   43: A \emph{context refinement} used below is a refinement
   44: \(\rho:\mathcal M'\to\mathcal M\) on the same measurements and outcomes,
   45: with \(C'\subseteq\rho(C')\), for which marginalization defines the refined
   46: model \(\rho^*e\). The inclusion of downward-closed context categories induces
   47: a functor
   48: \[
   49: u_\rho:\mathcal D_{\mathcal M'}\hookrightarrow
   50: \mathcal D_{\mathcal M}
   51: \]
   52: which is required to be continuous for the two generated cover topologies and
   53: to extend to their terminal augmentations. We also require the natural
   54: base-change isomorphism
   55: \[
   56: S_{\rho^*e}\cong u_\rho^*S_e.
   57: \]
   58: This includes ordinary iterated refinements which are covering refinements
   59: for the generated topology. No
   60: claim is made here for resource-theoretic simulations which change the
   61: measurement or outcome sets.
   62: 
   63: \begin{proposition}[Abramsky--Brandenburger support interface]\label{prop:ab-compatibility-translation}
   64: For every finite empirical model \(e\), the following sets are naturally in
   65: bijection:
   66: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
   67: \item compatible families \((s_C)_{C\in\mathcal M}\) with
   68:       \(s_C\in S_e(C)\);
   69: \item global assignments \(s\in\prod_{x\in X}O_x\) such that
   70:       \(s|_C\in S_e(C)\) for every \(C\in\mathcal M\);
   71: \item global sections of the support presheaf in the standard
   72:       Abramsky--Brandenburger sense;
   73: \item elements of \(\widehat S_e(X)\), equivalently elements of
   74:       \((aS_e)(X)\) on the terminally augmented context site.
   75: \end{enumerate}
   76: Consequently, if both \(\CompSec_s(r)\) and \(\Sec_s(r)\) are interpreted
   77: from this same support presheaf on the standard measurement cover, then
   78: \[
   79: M,p\Vdash\CompSec_s(r)
   80: \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   81: M,p\Vdash\Sec_s(r).
   82: \]
   83: In particular, strong contextuality is absence of a compatible family at the
   84: set-valued level; it is not the gluing-level mode
   85: \(\CompSec_s(r)\land\neg\Sec_s(r)\) of this paper.
   86: \end{proposition}
   87: 
   88: \begin{proof}
   89: The event presheaf
   90: \(\mathcal E(U)=\prod_{x\in U}O_x\) is a sheaf. Hence a compatible family
   91: \((s_C)\) glues uniquely to a global assignment \(s\), and its restrictions
   92: remain in the prescribed supports. Conversely, restriction of such an
   93: assignment gives a compatible supported family. This proves the first three
   94: identifications. The fourth is the defining limit formula for
   95: \(\widehat S_e(X)\); the plus construction for the cover
   96: \(\mathcal M\to X\) gives the same set in the sheafification. The displayed
   97: equivalence follows immediately.
   98: \end{proof}
   99: 
  100: \begin{remark}[Support versus probabilistic contextuality]\label{rem:support-vs-probabilistic-contextuality}
  101: The proposition concerns the possibilistic support of \(e\). Probabilistic
  102: noncontextuality asks instead for a distribution on
  103: \(\prod_{x\in X}O_x\) whose marginals are the given distributions \(e_C\).
  104: That is a fibre-extension problem for the distribution presheaf, and is not
  105: determined by \(S_e\): empirical models with the same support can have
  106: different probabilistic noncontextuality behaviour.
  107: \end{remark}
  108: 
  109: \begin{theorem}[Canonical split stack and the degree obstruction]\label{thm:empirical-model-stack-interface}
  110: Let \(e\) be a finite empirical model on the context site above.
  111: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
  112: \item There is a canonical realization-stack extension with zero band,
  113: \[
  114: \mathfrak E_e^0:=\operatorname{Disc}(aS_e),
  115: \qquad
  116: \pi_0(\mathfrak E_e^0)\cong aS_e.
  117: \]
  118: Here \(\operatorname{Disc}\) regards a sheaf of sets as a stack of discrete
  119: groupoids.
  120: \item More generally, after an abelian sheaf \(\Band\) has been supplied,
  121: there is a canonical split \(\Band\)-banded extension
  122: \[
  123: \mathfrak E_e^{\mathrm{spl}}:=
  124: \operatorname{Disc}(aS_e)\times\mathsf B\Band.
  125: \]
  126: Every component gerbe of this extension is neutral, and therefore every
  127: Giraud class supplied by
  128: \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} is zero.
  129: \item The assignments in \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} are pseudonatural
  130: under context refinements: there are coherent banded equivalences
  131: \[
  132: u_\rho^{-1}\mathfrak E_e^0\simeq
  133: \mathfrak E_{\rho^*e}^0,
  134: \qquad
  135: u_\rho^{-1}\mathfrak E_e^{\mathrm{spl}}\simeq
  136: \mathfrak E_{\rho^*e}^{\mathrm{spl}}
  137: \]
  138: in the second formula whenever the supplied bands are identified under
  139: pullback.
  140: \item The AB and AMB constructions do not produce the non-split degree-two
  141: data required by this paper. More precisely, fix
  142: \(C_0\in\mathcal M\) and \(s\in S_e(C_0)\).
  143: Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa form the free-abelian presheaf
  144: \(\mathcal F_e=\mathbb Z[S_e]\), its relative kernel
  145: \(\mathcal F_{e,\overline C_0}\), and a class
  146: \[
  147: \gamma_e(s)\in
  148: \check H^1(\mathcal M,\mathcal F_{e,\overline C_0}).
  149: \]
  150: This is relative \v{C}ech cohomology of a presheaf, and the class is the
  151: isomorphism class of an
  152: \(\mathcal F_{e,\overline C_0}\)-torsor trivialized by
  153: \(\mathcal M\). It is not a derived \(H^2\) Giraud class for a sheaf band
  154: \cite{AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,Caru2017}.
  155: \item There is no comparison which recovers these AMB classes, for all finite
  156: empirical models, from the branch map of any realization-stack extension
  157: whose component sheaf is \(aS_e\). Indeed, if \(e\) is strongly contextual,
  158: then
  159: \[
  160: (aS_e)(X)=\varnothing,
  161: \]
  162: so the branch map
  163: \[
  164: \delta_{\mathfrak E_e}:(aS_e)(X)\longrightarrow
  165: H^2(\mathcal D_{\mathcal M},\Band)
  166: \]
  167: has empty domain, whereas AMB classes are defined for the local sections
  168: \(s\in S_e(C_0)\) and can be nonzero, as in their GHZ and
  169: Kochen--Specker examples.
  170: \end{enumerate}
  171: In \textup{(i)}, \emph{canonical} means that the construction is the
  172: composite of the universal sheafification functor and the discrete-stack
  173: functor, with no choices, and that the displayed refinement equivalences
  174: satisfy the usual pseudofunctor coherence. It does not mean that all
  175: realization-stack extensions of \(S_e\) are equivalent.
  176: \end{theorem}
  177: 
  178: \begin{proof}
  179: The discrete groupoid construction preserves descent, so
  180: \(\operatorname{Disc}(aS_e)\) is a stack and its connected-component sheaf is
  181: exactly \(aS_e\). Its automorphism sheaves are zero, proving \textup{(i)}.
  182: The classifying stack \(\mathsf B\Band\) has one local component and
  183: automorphism sheaf \(\Band\). Taking its product with the discrete stack
  184: therefore proves the band and component assertions in \textup{(ii)}. The
  185: global object represented by the identity \(\Band\)-torsor neutralizes each
  186: component gerbe, so its Giraud class vanishes.
  187: 
  188: Inverse image for the morphism of context sites commutes, up to its canonical
  189: isomorphism, with associated sheaves, discrete stacks, products, and
  190: classifying stacks. Together with
  191: \(S_{\rho^*e}\cong u_\rho^*S_e\), this gives the equivalences and their
  192: coherence in \textup{(iii)}.
  193: 
  194: The construction of \(\gamma_e(s)\) and its degree are those of
  195: \cite[Sec.~4]{AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012}. The torsor
  196: classification is \cite[Prop.~6.3]{Caru2017}, proving \textup{(iv)}. Finally,
  197: \Cref{prop:ab-compatibility-translation} identifies strong contextuality with
  198: emptiness of \((aS_e)(X)\). The branch obstruction map of
  199: \Cref{thm:intrinsic-branch-obstruction-extension} is indexed by precisely
  200: that set, while \(\gamma_e(s)\) is indexed by a local section. This proves
  201: the asserted failure in \textup{(v)}.
  202: \end{proof}
  203: 
  204: \begin{corollary}[Exact limit of transfer to empirical models]\label{thm:unique-branch-contextuality-comparison}
  205: For finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical models, the set-valued
  206: local-to-global statements of \Cref{prop:ab-compatibility-translation}
  207: transfer functorially. The later banded and homological theorems transfer
  208: only after a band and a non-split realization-stack extension have been
  209: supplied as additional data. In particular:
  210: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
  211: \item the canonical split extension gives only zero Giraud classes and zero
  212: hidden subgroups;
  213: \item the characterization
  214: \[
  215: d(G)\le 2\beta
  216: \quad\text{and}\quad
  217: G\text{ is not a cyclic }p\text{-group}
  218: \]
  219: remains a realization theorem for the chosen bouquet good-cover, band, and
  220: two-branch cocycle data of
  221: \Cref{thm:bouquet-two-branch-resolution}; it is not a characterization of
  222: groups canonically attached to empirical models;
  223: \item without an additional degree-shifting construction, the Giraud
  224: \(H^2\)-class neither recovers nor refines the AMB relative
  225: \(\check H^1\)-obstruction.
  226: \end{enumerate}
  227: \end{corollary}
  228: 
  229: \begin{proof}
  230: The first and third assertions are
  231: \Cref{thm:empirical-model-stack-interface}(ii),(iv)--(v). The bouquet theorem
  232: starts from a prescribed finite nerve, a constant finite abelian band, and
  233: chosen branchwise homomorphisms
  234: \(H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A\). None of those data is selected by a bare empirical
  235: model, so its group classification cannot be transported through the split
  236: construction. This proves the second assertion.

 succeeded in 203ms:
  121: Under the additional direct-sum hypotheses, the branch-sensitive hidden
  122: subgroup intersection is $0$ and the branch-uniform hidden subgroup sum
  123: is all of $G$. The quotient formulas in
  124: \Cref{thm:branch-sensitive-visible-quotient,thm:branch-uniform-visible-quotient,thm:branch-comparison-exact-sequence}
  125: therefore give
  126: \[
  127: A_{\mathrm{vis}}^{\mathrm{br}}(r)\cong B_{\mathrm{res}}(r)\cong G,
  128: \qquad
  129: A_{\mathrm{vis}}^{\mathrm{unif}}(r)=0.
  130: \]
  131: Finally, because both branches are non-neutral,
  132: \Cref{thm:mixed-branch-realization}(iv) gives
  133: $M,p\Vdash \Null_s^{\mathrm{glue}}(r)$.
  134: \end{proof}

  136: \begin{theorem}[Admissible-expansion two-branch resolution on chosen bouquet good covers]\label{thm:bouquet-two-branch-resolution}
  137: Fix an integer $\beta\ge 1$, let $K_\beta$ be a finite connected simplicial complex whose geometric realization is homotopy equivalent to
  138: \[
  139: \bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta} S^2,
  140: \]
  141: and write
  142: \[
  143: X_\beta:=|K_\beta|.
  144: \]
  145: For each $m\ge 0$, let
  146: \[
  147: \mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}
  148: \]
  149: be the open-star cover of the barycentric subdivision $\operatorname{Sd}^m K_\beta$, viewed as a cover of $X_\beta$. Let $\mathcal C_a$ be the pullback site whose objects are $X_\beta$, a strict initial object $\emptyset$, and all nonempty finite intersections of members of the covers $\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}$; the pullback of two objects over a common target is their nonempty intersection when it is nonempty and is $\emptyset$ otherwise. Covering families are generated by the families $\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}$, their pullbacks, identity covers, and the empty cover of $\emptyset$.
  150: All admissible-expansion realization assertions in this theorem are understood relative to the
  151: well-typed admissible-expansion convention of
  152: \Cref{prop:admissible-layer-expansion-interface}.
  153: 
  154: Then the family
  155: \[
  156: \bigl(\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}\bigr)_{m\ge 0}
  157: \]
  158: is a filtered cofinal family satisfying \textup{(H4)} for every constant finite abelian band.
  159: 
  160: Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, and write $d(G)$ for the minimal number of generators of $G$. Then the following are equivalent.
  161: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
  162: \item $G\ne0$, $d(G)\le 2\beta$, and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group, where
  163: cyclic $p$-group means cyclic of order $p^n$ with $n\ge1$.
  164: \item In the admissible-expansion model class generated by
  165: \Cref{prop:admissible-layer-expansion-interface}, the one-state
  166: \(\mathbb L_1\)-reduct, the site \(\mathcal C_a\), a local object functor on
  167: \(\mathcal C_a\), and a realization prestack
  168: \[
  169: \mathfrak P_r\to \mathcal C_a
  170: \]
  171: with trivialized constant band $G$ define a one-state
  172: \(\mathbb L_2/\mathbb L_3\) model \(M\) with state \(p\) and admitted
  173: reference \(r:\mathsf{Ref}_s\), \(a=[r]_p\), using the finite-nerve Leray
  174: comparison supplied by the chosen bouquet good covers, such that
  175: \[
  176: \Vis_{p,s}(r)=\{v_1,v_2\},
  177: \]
  178: both component gerbes $\mathfrak G_{v_1}$ and $\mathfrak G_{v_2}$ are non-neutral, and
  179: \[
  180: K_{v_1}\cap K_{v_2}=0,
  181: \qquad
  182: K_{v_1}+K_{v_2}=G.
  183: \]
  184: \end{enumerate}
  185: Whenever these conditions hold,
  186: \[
  187: A_{\mathrm{vis}}^{\mathrm{br}}(r)\cong B_{\mathrm{res}}(r)\cong G,
  188: \qquad
  189: A_{\mathrm{vis}}^{\mathrm{unif}}(r)=0,
  190: \qquad
  191: M,p\Vdash \Null_s^{\mathrm{glue}}(r).
  192: \]
  193: \end{theorem}
  194: 
  195: \begin{proof}
  196: We use four explicit interfaces: the good-cover comparison, the
  197: finite-abelian decomposition, the mixed-realization transfer, and the
  198: branch-exactness consequence.
  199: 
  200: The good-cover interface is supplied by
  201: \Cref{lem:bouquet-cover-classical-interface}. By clause \textup{(i)},
  202: each $\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}$ is a finite good cover of $X_\beta$, its
  203: nonempty finite intersections are contractible, and
  204: \[
  205: N(\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)})\cong \operatorname{Sd}^{m}K_\beta.
  206: \]
  207: Thus the constant band $G$ is trivial on every such cover, and
  208: \[
  209: H^1(U_{i_0\cdots i_n},G)=0
  210: \]
  211: for every nonempty intersection appearing in the \v{C}ech descent
  212: argument. Clause \textup{(ii)} makes
  213: $\bigl(\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}\bigr)_{m\ge 0}$ filtered and cofinal in the
  214: generated pretopology of $\mathcal C_a$, and clause \textup{(iii)}
  215: identifies the filtered \v{C}ech system with derived cohomology. Hence
  216: the family satisfies \textup{(H4)} for every constant finite abelian band.
  217: 
  218: Also, every subdivision of $K_\beta$ is homotopy equivalent to $K_\beta$, hence
  219: \[
  220: H_1\bigl(N(\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}),\mathbb Z\bigr)=0,
  221: \qquad
  222: H_2\bigl(N(\mathcal U_\beta^{(m)}),\mathbb Z\bigr)\cong \mathbb Z^\beta
  223: \]
  224: for every $m$ \cite[Secs.~2.1, 2.2]{Hatcher2002}. This records exactly
  225: the finite-nerve hypotheses needed by the realization theorems.
  226: 
  227: Now assume \textup{(i)}. The finite-abelian interface is
  228: \Cref{lem:bouquet-cover-classical-interface}(iv): it gives a direct-sum
  229: decomposition
  230: \[
  231: G=G_1\oplus G_2
  232: \]
  233: with $G_1,G_2$ nonzero and
  234: \[
  235: d(G_1)\le\beta,
  236: \qquad
  237: d(G_2)\le\beta.
  238: \]
  239: The mixed-realization transfer
  240: \Cref{lem:bouquet-mixed-realization-transfer} applied to these two
  241: summands produces a realization with two visible branches, non-neutral
  242: component gerbes, and $K_{v_i}=G_i$. Because the summands form an
  243: internal direct sum, $G_1\cap G_2=0$ and $G_1+G_2=G$, so condition
  244: \textup{(ii)} follows.
  245: 
  246: Conversely, assume \textup{(ii)} and put
  247: \[
  248: K_i:=K_{v_i}
  249: \qquad
  250: (i=1,2).
  251: \]
  252: For each $i$, choose a finite nerve presentation of the branch class $\omega_{v_i}$ on one of the covers $\mathcal U_\beta^{(m_i)}$. Since the good-cover interface gives
  253: \[
  254: H_2\bigl(N(\mathcal U_\beta^{(m_i)}),\mathbb Z\bigr)\cong \mathbb Z^\beta,
  255: \]
  256: the hidden subgroup
  257: \[
  258: K_i=\operatorname{Im}(\mathrm{ev}_{\omega_{v_i}})
  259: \]
  260: is generated by at most $\beta$ elements. The equalities
  261: \[
  262: K_1\cap K_2=0,
  263: \qquad
  264: K_1+K_2=G
  265: \]
  266: give an internal direct-sum decomposition
  267: \[
  268: G\cong K_1\oplus K_2
  269: \]
  270: with both summands nonzero. Hence $G$ is decomposable, and the finite abelian indecomposable groups are exactly the cyclic $p$-groups \cite[Chap.~12]{DummitFoote2004}. Moreover
  271: \[
  272: d(G)\le d(K_1)+d(K_2)\le 2\beta.
  273: \]
  274: Thus \textup{(i)} holds.
  275: 
  276: Finally, the exact-sequence consequences are separate from the realization step. The identities
  277: \[
  278: \bigcap_{i=1}^2 K_{v_i}=0,
  279: \qquad
  280: \sum_{i=1}^2 K_{v_i}=G
  281: \]
  282: give
  283: \[
  284: A_{\mathrm{vis}}^{\mathrm{br}}(r)\cong B_{\mathrm{res}}(r)\cong G,
  285: \qquad
  286: A_{\mathrm{vis}}^{\mathrm{unif}}(r)=0
  287: \]
  288: by \Cref{thm:branch-sensitive-visible-quotient,thm:branch-uniform-visible-quotient,thm:branch-comparison-exact-sequence}. Since both branches are non-neutral, \Cref{thm:mixed-branch-realization}(iv) gives
  289: \[
  290: M,p\Vdash \Null_s^{\mathrm{glue}}(r).
  291: \]
  292: \end{proof}
  293:

 \begin{abstract}
-We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a Giraud class in $H^2$. Every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical refinement-functorial split extension, but all its Giraud classes vanish; the Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction is instead a relative $H^1$ torsor class indexed by a local section. Thus the banded theory requires extra lift data. For finite abelian bands its homological evaluation map controls a presentation-object visible quotient. On bouquet good covers, a nonzero finite abelian group occurs as a pure two-branch resolution kernel exactly when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group, but this classification does not canonically transfer to empirical models.
+A nonzero finite abelian group $G$ occurs as a two-component label-loss kernel with complementary nonzero image subgroups on the chosen good-cover site of a wedge of $\beta$ copies of $S^2$ if and only if $d(G)\leq 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group.  This follows from the universal coefficient theorem after fixing a finite nerve, a constant finite abelian band, and a banded groupoid lift of a presheaf.  For a component-gerbe class $\omega$, evaluation on $H_2$ gives $\operatorname{ev}_\omega:H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A$; its image and cokernel determine the componentwise and aggregate quotients.  When $H_1(N,\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^\beta$, the possible image subgroups are exactly those generated by at most $\beta$ elements.  Under explicit separatedness, representability, and \v{C}ech-to-derived comparison hypotheses, matching families without global amalgamations correspond to non-neutral component gerbes.  This derived $H^2$ invariant is not the relative \v{C}ech $H^1$ obstruction of Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa; only the underlying support-presheaf comparison is functorial.
 \end{abstract}

 \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
 
-Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
+Fix an integer $\beta\geq 1$.  Our main classification theorem concerns the
+good-cover intersection site obtained from barycentric open-star covers of a
+finite model of the wedge $\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2$.  A nonzero finite
+abelian group $G$ occurs as the kernel of the canonical map
+\[
+ A/\bigl(K_1\cap K_2\bigr)\longrightarrow A/\bigl(K_1+K_2\bigr)
+\]
+for two non-neutral component gerbes with $K_1\cap K_2=0$ and
+$K_1+K_2=G$ if and only if
+\[
+ d(G)\leq 2\beta
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ G\text{ is not a cyclic }p\text{-group}.
+\]
+Here $d(G)$ is the minimal number of generators of $G$.  In the terminology
+fixed below, this kernel is the \emph{component-forgetting kernel}; the
+displayed special case is a two-component label-loss kernel with complementary
+nonzero image subgroups.  The statement is an existence and classification
+result for the chosen site, band, and lift data, not an invariant of an
+arbitrary empirical model.

-The first part of the paper concerns the passage from information states to local objects. \Cref{prop:compsec-to-sheafification} shows that compatible local sectionability gives nonemptiness of the associated sheafification, and \Cref{thm:sheafification-characterization} proves the converse on slice-separated reference slices. +We now describe the framework.  An information state
+$p=(\Gamma_p,R_p)$ is a nonempty team $R_p$ of assignments with common finite

-The sheaf-theoretic, gerbe-theoretic, and homological tools used here are classical, and several of the later comparison results are formal once the branchwise intrinsic data have been fixed. +\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=0pt,labelindent=0pt]
+\item[Information state $p=(\Gamma,R)$.]
+A nonempty team $R$ of assignments with common finite context $\Gamma$.
+\item[Universal team satisfaction.]
+$M,p\Vdash\varphi$ means that every assignment in the team of $p$ satisfies
+$\varphi$ in ordinary Tarskian semantics.
+\item[Singleton-state embedding.]
+The map from an assignment to its singleton team, preserving ordinary
+satisfaction.
+\item[Truth-preserving reduct expansion.]
+An expansion whose higher models preserve lower-language satisfaction after
+the specified model reduct and state projection; consequence conservativity
+is not part of the definition.
+\item[Typed expansion class.]
+The class of all supplied higher-layer data of the stipulated types over a
+fixed lower model.
+\item[Admissible parameter $r$.]
+An element satisfying the primitive predicate $\Adm_s$; the predicate records
+exactly that the site and presheaf data stipulated in the relevant typed model
+are attached to $r$.
+\item[Base object $a=[r]_p$.]
+The object of the reference-refinement site associated to the pair $(p,r)$;
+the brackets do not denote an equivalence class.
+\item[Reference-refinement site $\mathcal C_{p,s}$.]
+The thin category of base objects ordered by refinement, equipped with the
+specified pretopology and pullbacks.
+\item[Presheaf of local sections $F_{p,s}$.]
+The functor $\mathcal C_{p,s}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$.
+\item[Matching without amalgamation at $a$.]
+A matching family exists on a cover of $a$, but $F_{p,s}(a)$ is empty.
+\item[Gluing-sensitive banded lift datum.]
+A banded groupoid lift, its stackification and component-sheaf identification,
+terminal-fibre essential surjectivity, and a \v{C}ech-to-derived comparison
+hypothesis.
+\item[Pullback-stable representative choice.]
+A choice of one representative of each presheaf section that is preserved
+strictly by every pullback; ``representative-rigid'' abbreviates this condition.
+\item[Global component section $v$.]
+An element of $\pi_0(\mathfrak L_r)(a)$, identified with a section of
+$(aF)(a)$.
+\item[Component gerbe $\mathfrak G_v$ and component obstruction $\omega_v$.]
+The full banded substack over $v$ and its Giraud class
+$[\mathfrak G_v]\in H^2(\mathcal C/a,\Band)$.
+\item[Presentation-comparison groupoid.]
+The groupoid freely generated by the specified refinements, cocycle
+replacements, band retrivializations, and their formal inverses; distinct
+zigzags need not give the same comparison.
+\item[Coordinate-image subgroup and cocycle-coordinate quotient.]
+For a chosen cocycle $\alpha$, the subgroup generated by its coordinate values
+and the corresponding quotient $A/H_\alpha$.
+\item[Homological image $K_\omega$ and homological cokernel $Q_\omega$.]
+$\operatorname{Im}(\operatorname{ev}_\omega)$ and
+$\operatorname{coker}(\operatorname{ev}_\omega)=A/K_\omega$.
+\item[Label-aware quotient.]
+$A/(\bigcap_vK_v)$, equivalently the image of $A$ in the product of the
+componentwise homological cokernels.
+\item[Common-character quotient.]
+$A/(\sum_vK_v)$, detected by the characters that annihilate every $K_v$.
+\item[Component-forgetting kernel.]
+The kernel of the canonical map from the label-aware quotient to the
+common-character quotient, namely $(\sum_vK_v)/(\bigcap_vK_v)$.
+\item[Fibre-separating auxiliary register.]
+A finite set used in an injective lift of a quotient map; its minimum
+cardinality is the largest quotient-fibre cardinality.
+\item[Finite intersection site associated to a cover nerve.]
+The finite thin pullback site generated by the formal intersections indexed by
+the nerve, with an initial object representing empty intersections.
+\end{description}

 \begin{abstract}
-We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct.  \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
 
-Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
+Fix an integer $\beta\geq 1$.  Our main classification theorem concerns the
+good-cover intersection site obtained from barycentric open-star covers of a
+finite model of the wedge $\bigvee_{j=1}^{\beta}S^2$.  A nonzero finite
+abelian group $G$ occurs as the kernel of the canonical map
+\[
+ A/\bigl(K_1\cap K_2\bigr)\longrightarrow A/\bigl(K_1+K_2\bigr)
+\]
+for two non-neutral component gerbes with $K_1\cap K_2=0$ and
+$K_1+K_2=G$ if and only if
+\[
+ d(G)\leq 2\beta
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ G\text{ is not a cyclic }p\text{-group}.

-The first part of the paper concerns the passage from information states to local objects. \Cref{prop:compsec-to-sheafification} shows that compatible local sectionability gives nonemptiness of the associated sheafification, and \Cref{thm:sheafification-characterization} proves the converse on slice-separated reference slices. +We now describe the framework.  An information state

+\subsection*{Glossary of retained terminology}
 
-The sheaf-theoretic, gerbe-theoretic, and homological tools used here are classical, and several of the later comparison results are formal once the branchwise intrinsic data have been fixed. +The following short names are used only after their standard-language content

-The paper is organized as follows. \Cref{sec:preliminaries} fixes the extension chain and the relevant notions of conservativity. \Cref{sec:information-states} recalls forcing over information states. \Cref{sec:null-decomposition} studies local objects, sheafification, and lower-fragment separation. \Cref{sec:gerbe-obstruction} introduces component gerbes and branch obstruction classes. \Cref{sec:homological-visibility} and \Cref{sec:branch-aggregation} contain the homological visibility theory together with the branchwise comparison and realization results. +\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=0pt,labelindent=0pt]
+\item[Information state $p=(\Gamma,R)$.]
+A nonempty team $R$ of assignments with common finite context $\Gamma$.
+\item[Universal team satisfaction.]
+$M,p\Vdash\varphi$ means that every assignment in the team of $p$ satisfies
+$\varphi$ in ordinary Tarskian semantics.
+\item[Singleton-state embedding.]
+The map from an assignment to its singleton team, preserving ordinary
+satisfaction.
+\item[Truth-preserving reduct expansion.]
+An expansion whose higher models preserve lower-language satisfaction after
+the specified model reduct and state projection; consequence conservativity
+is not part of the definition.
+\item[Typed expansion class.]
+The class of all supplied higher-layer data of the stipulated types over a
+fixed lower model.
+\item[Admissible parameter $r$.]
+An element satisfying the primitive predicate $\Adm_s$; the predicate records
+exactly that the site and presheaf data stipulated in the relevant typed model
+are attached to $r$.
+\item[Base object $a=[r]_p$.]
+The object of the reference-refinement site associated to the pair $(p,r)$;
+the brackets do not denote an equivalence class.
+\item[Reference-refinement site $\mathcal C_{p,s}$.]
+The thin category of base objects ordered by refinement, equipped with the
+specified pretopology and pullbacks.
+\item[Presheaf of local sections $F_{p,s}$.]
+The functor $\mathcal C_{p,s}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$.
+\item[Matching without amalgamation at $a$.]
+A matching family exists on a cover of $a$, but $F_{p,s}(a)$ is empty.
+\item[Gluing-sensitive banded lift datum.]
+A banded groupoid lift, its stackification and component-sheaf identification,
+terminal-fibre essential surjectivity, and a \v{C}ech-to-derived comparison
+hypothesis.
+\item[Pullback-stable representative choice.]
+A choice of one representative of each presheaf section that is preserved
+strictly by every pullback; ``representative-rigid'' abbreviates this condition.
+\item[Global component section $v$.]
+An element of $\pi_0(\mathfrak L_r)(a)$, identified with a section of
+$(aF)(a)$.
+\item[Component gerbe $\mathfrak G_v$ and component obstruction $\omega_v$.]
+The full banded substack over $v$ and its Giraud class
+$[\mathfrak G_v]\in H^2(\mathcal C/a,\Band)$.
+\item[Presentation-comparison groupoid.]
+The groupoid freely generated by the specified refinements, cocycle
+replacements, band retrivializations, and their formal inverses; distinct
+zigzags need not give the same comparison.
+\item[Coordinate-image subgroup and cocycle-coordinate quotient.]
+For a chosen cocycle $\alpha$, the subgroup generated by its coordinate values
+and the corresponding quotient $A/H_\alpha$.
+\item[Homological image $K_\omega$ and homological cokernel $Q_\omega$.]
+$\operatorname{Im}(\operatorname{ev}_\omega)$ and
+$\operatorname{coker}(\operatorname{ev}_\omega)=A/K_\omega$.
+\item[Label-aware quotient.]
+$A/(\bigcap_vK_v)$, equivalently the image of $A$ in the product of the
+componentwise homological cokernels.
+\item[Common-character quotient.]
+$A/(\sum_vK_v)$, detected by the characters that annihilate every $K_v$.
+\item[Component-forgetting kernel.]
+The kernel of the canonical map from the label-aware quotient to the
+common-character quotient, namely $(\sum_vK_v)/(\bigcap_vK_v)$.
+\item[Fibre-separating auxiliary register.]
+A finite set used in an injective lift of a quotient map; its minimum
+cardinality is the largest quotient-fibre cardinality.
+\item[Finite intersection site associated to a cover nerve.]
+The finite thin pullback site generated by the formal intersections indexed by
+the nerve, with an initial object representing empty intersections.
+\end{description}

 \begin{abstract}
-We study gluing failure in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations. For admitted references, compatible local sectionability is equivalent, on slice-separated reference slices, to nonemptiness of the sheafification of the associated local-object functor. A lower-fragment separation theorem shows that compatible local sections, global sections, and gluing-level nullity are undefinable in the automorphism-invariant, constant-free, one-variable fragment of the lower reduct. At the groupoid-valued level, representative rigidity and global conservativity force surjectivity of the sheafification unit at the terminal fibre. For banded realization-stack extensions, each visible branch determines a Giraud class in $H^2$. Every finite Abramsky--Brandenburger empirical model has a canonical refinement-functorial split extension, but all its Giraud classes vanish; the Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa obstruction is instead a relative $H^1$ torsor class indexed by a local section. Thus the banded theory requires extra lift data. For finite abelian bands its homological evaluation map controls a presentation-object visible quotient. On bouquet good covers, a nonzero finite abelian group occurs as a pure two-branch resolution kernel exactly when $d(G)\le 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group, but this classification does not canonically transfer to empirical models.
+A nonzero finite abelian group $G$ occurs as a two-component label-loss kernel with complementary nonzero image subgroups on the chosen good-cover site of a wedge of $\beta$ copies of $S^2$ if and only if $d(G)\leq 2\beta$ and $G$ is not a cyclic $p$-group.  This follows from the universal coefficient theorem after fixing a finite nerve, a constant finite abelian band, and a banded groupoid lift of a presheaf.  For a component-gerbe class $\omega$, evaluation on $H_2$ gives $\operatorname{ev}_\omega:H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\to A$; its image and cokernel determine the componentwise and aggregate quotients.  When $H_1(N,\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H_2(N,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^\beta$, the possible image subgroups are exactly those generated by at most $\beta$ elements.  Under explicit separatedness, representability, and \v{C}ech-to-derived comparison hypotheses, matching families without global amalgamations correspond to non-neutral component gerbes.  This derived $H^2$ invariant is not the relative \v{C}ech $H^1$ obstruction of Abramsky--Mansfield--Barbosa; only the underlying support-presheaf comparison is functorial.
 \end{abstract}

 \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
 
-Sheaf-theoretic semantics offers a natural language for the passage from local data to global objects. In logical applications, and in particular in sheaf-theoretic analyses of contextuality \cite{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldSoaresBarbosa2012,AbramskyBarbosaKishidaLalMansfield2015,Caru2017,Caru2018,Montanhano2021}, the central question is whether compatible local families glue to global sections. The classical tools for measuring the failure of gluing are gerbes, obstruction classes, and cohomological invariants \cite{Giraud1971,Breen2006,Hatcher2002}. In this paper we study that question in a forcing semantics whose states are sets of realizations, with the aim of separating the successive layers at which genuinely new local-to-global structure appears.
+Fix an integer $\beta\geq 1$.  Our main classification theorem concerns the
